| [THEORY-075](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-075.md) | Moral obligation follows from valuing humanity | Korsgaard (1992), [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md): because human consciousness is reflective, an agent must act on reasons, and so must identify with some law, a "practical identity": "a description under which you value yourself". "Your reasons express your identity, your nature; your obligations spring from what that identity forbids." Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity", unconditional where violation would be worse than death. Identities are a "jumble" and differ across social worlds, so this much yields no morality. Moral obligation enters because valuing any identity requires valuing one's humanity, the source of all one's reasons. "The Normative Constitution of Agency" ([LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md)) later makes practical identity the content of maxims chosen under the formal norms. Argued, with the key steps flagged by their author as sketchy; the commentaries and reply are unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-118](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-118.md) | Praise fits determinism; blame needs alternatives | Susan Wolf's asymmetry thesis, reported second-hand: the primary texts are unread. McKenna and Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md), §4.3), citing "Asymmetrical Freedom" and Freedom Within Reason pp. 79–81, report that for Wolf praiseworthy conduct does not require the freedom to do otherwise and blameworthy conduct does. An agent determined to act in accord with the True and the Good loses nothing by lacking the ability to act irrationally; an agent who acts against it and cannot act in accord with it cannot reasonably be blamed. In Fischer's terms, only blame needs regulative control. Wolf holds that the ability needs only the falsity of psychological, not physical, determinism. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-119](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-119.md) v2 | The alternate possibilities principle is false | Frankfurt (1969, [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md), read): Black stands ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needs to, so Jones4 could not have done otherwise and is as responsible, for blame or praise, as without Black. | [THEORY-120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-120.md) v2 | Free will is identification with one's motives | Frankfurt's hierarchical, or endorsement, account, from his own texts: the 1971 paper ([LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md), read) and the 2004 Tanner Lectures ([LIT-293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-293.md), read). A person's will is the desire that moves him to act; he identifies with a desire by wanting it to be his will, decisively, and he acts of his own free will when the will that moves him is the will he wants. In 2004 the condition is "volitional unanimity" with no conflict "at any higher order", and identification is "willing acceptance", which may be resigned. Acting of one's own free will is what responsibility requires, and alternatives and history are irrelevant. The 1987 and 1992 revisions are held only by report. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-121](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-121.md) v7 | Guidance control suffices for responsibility | Fischer and Ravizza, in their own précis ([LIT-728](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-728.md), read): moral responsibility requires guidance control, not regulative control over alternatives. Fischer's 1987 paper ([LIT-687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-687.md), read) is the weak-responsiveness origin. The view is compatible with causal determinism. | Active |
| [THEORY-122](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-122.md) v2 | Responsibility needs normative competence | Susan Wolf's Reason View, reported second-hand: the primary texts are unread. McKenna and Coates ([LIT-291](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-291.md), §4.3) report that for Wolf free will is the ability to act in accord with the True and the Good, an anchor outside the agent's psychology. Talbert ([LIT-691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-691.md), §§3.1.1, 3.2) reports her case against deep-self or Real Self views and the JoJo case: JoJo identifies wholly with the cruel values his father raised him in, yet is not responsible, because he cannot appreciate that they are wrong. The claim is a necessary condition. It does not by itself say whether the ability must include being able to do otherwise; that is [THEORY-118](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-118.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-207](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-207.md) v2 | Network harms can be allocated without fault | Floridi (2016), [LIT-899](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-899.md), read in [NOTE-699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-699.md). A distributed moral action is an outcome no one intended. Floridi proposes holding every causally accountable node "prima facie equally and maximally responsible", overridably, with the rule publicly announced so that agents restrain one another. Proposed: the rule is a design argued by analogy and by two court cases. In one of those cases the default is overridden by ease of rectification, which is a control criterion. It does not show that what is allocated is moral responsibility rather than accountability used as a corrective signal. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-225](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-225.md) | No single mechanism defines manipulation | Noggle, SEP (2018, rev. 2026), [LIT-1007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1007.md), §§2.1–2.4, read in full in [NOTE-744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-744.md). | [THEORY-235](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-235.md) | Covert exploitation always harms autonomy | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum (2019), [LIT-1002](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1002.md), pp. 4–5 and 9–11, read in full in [NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md). | [THEORY-258](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-258.md) | Feedback optimization targets vulnerable users | Williams et al. | [THEORY-326](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-326.md) v2 | Hermeneutical injustice needs no powerless group | Fricker (2006), "Powerlessness and Social Interpretation" ([LIT-1046](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1046.md), [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md)), drawn by her own note from the book's final chapter, with her 2017 restatement ([LIT-1048](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1048.md), [NOTE-853](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-853.md)). | [THEORY-428](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-428.md) | Ritual protest can be harmonizing incivility | Walsh (2021), [LIT-209](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-209.md), read in [NOTE-164](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-164.md) from the accepted manuscript. | [THEORY-464](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-464.md) v2 | Ethics turns on relations other than identity | Dufner (2025), [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md), the SEP entry that replaced Shoemaker's, read in [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md). | [THEORY-467](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-467.md) | Rule-consequentialism doesn't collapse into act | Hooker, SEP "Rule Consequentialism" (2003, revised 2023), [LIT-198](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-198.md), read in [NOTE-160](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-160.md). | [THEORY-525](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-525.md) | Refusing persona change denies recognition | Archer & Robb (2025), [LIT-172](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-172.md), read in [NOTE-186](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-186.md). Informal argument from one main case (Taylor Swift, 2018). The duties derived are fans' only, though the abstract promises celebrities' too. It needs a person on the far side, so it does not carry over to AI companions without an argument about their moral status. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-540](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-540.md) | BCI software can be a body part, server not | Register (2025), [LIT-138](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-138.md), read in full in [NOTE-151](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-151.md). An argument from cases. It assumes that BCIs can be body parts and that no part of a person may be owned by another, and uses depth to reconcile the user's unqualified bodily ownership with the operator's property in the server. The two moral principles are its operative premises, and it says they do not depend on the real-definition ontology, which only explains them. The threshold for "high-level" is context-sensitive and unfixed, and the step that software and server are distinct coinciding objects is hedged. The conflict over servers is narrowed, not dissolved. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-554](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-554.md) v2 | Standing grounds don't secure human priority | Schwitzgebel & Sinnott-Armstrong (2026), [LIT-166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md) ([NOTE-116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-116.md)), with the SEP survey of animal moral status ([LIT-146](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-146.md), [NOTE-181](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-181.md)) for the failure of capacity-based human exceptionalism. | [THEORY-561](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-561.md) | Moral thresholds make group good non-additive | Floridi (2013), [LIT-901](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-901.md), read in [NOTE-698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-698.md). A model with two moral thresholds and four positive examples; it proves nothing and reports no data. That morally loaded wholes can arise from negligible parts follows once thresholds are granted, and the reading rates it moderate. The analogy with distributed knowledge is inexact: every example sums like contributions, the threshold's value is left open, and so the line between distributed morality and a sum of loaded acts is a free parameter. Responsibility for such outcomes is not given here. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-600](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-600.md) | Justice alone can't define disease | Veit (2025), [LIT-098](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-098.md), read in [NOTE-097](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-097.md) from the PhilSci-Archive preprint. The target is Kukla's institutional definition: a condition is a health condition iff medicalising it would be best for collective wellbeing. The argument is informal and has two horns. One is a thought experiment (p. 14). The other rests on an asserted, undocumented premise about how medical tools evolve (p. 15). The extension from Kukla to "any purely normativist account" is asserted, not shown case by case. Veit concedes the first horn bites only without moral consensus. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-627](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-627.md) | Learned nudges need cognitive inspection | Schmauder et al. | [THEORY-667](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-667.md) | Gender and race are hierarchical positions | Haslanger (2000), [LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md), read in [NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md). Its empirical premises about race are uncited. Not a discovery about bodies, and not a claim that every female is a woman in its sense. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-677](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-677.md) | Precaution alone can't settle sentience errors | Schwitzgebel & Sinnott-Armstrong (2026), [LIT-166](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-166.md), read in [NOTE-116](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-116.md) from the September 2025 draft. A conceptual argument with worked cases, which the reading rates strong: "By itself, an appeal to precaution does not specify the type of error most to be avoided" (p. 8). Birch's framework puts the burden on whoever risks harming a sentience candidate; Mill's harm principle, read as a precaution, puts it on whoever would restrict liberty. The record holds the point, not the reviewers' reading of Birch's books, which it has not read. | Active |
| [THEORY-684](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-684.md) | Narrativity isn't needed for a good life | Strawson (2004), [LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md), read in [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md). It does not say that the remoter past did not happen to the human being, only to the self one now experiences oneself to be, and that metaphysical claim is asserted from earlier papers. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-699](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-699.md) v2 | Insentient self-maintainers have a good | Bruckner (2025), [LIT-120](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-120.md), read in [NOTE-093](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-093.md). Proposed by abduction from agreed cases, not deduced (§4): an entity that "sustains, maintains, and renews itself in a way that responds and adapts to its environmental conditions" is a welfare subject. Plants and the hypothetical car Tessler qualify; governors, thermostats and missiles do not. The "autopoiesis" is a loose behavioural notion, not Maturana and Varela's self-production, and the thermostat line is supported only comparatively. The answer to absurd obligations borrows Bradford 2023 and makes phenomenal consciousness decide how much such welfare matters. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-864](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-864.md) | AI testimonial injustice via credibility excess | Kay, Kasirzadeh and Mohamed (2024), [LIT-1338](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1338.md), read in [NOTE-1049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1049.md): "In the algorithmic setting, the injustice requires a credibility excess assigned to the algorithm". A conceptual analysis, illustrated with reported cases. It does not say that users do overtrust models (the paper measures nothing), that deliberate fabrication is testimonial injustice in Fricker's sense, or that the amplification is a loop with any stated condition. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1173](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1173.md) | Testimonial injustice is unwitting prejudice | The wide form [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md) held before the twelfth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-327](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-327.md), Active, is its evidence. Fricker states the account as what testimonial injustice is, not only as her usage; the record holds it as hers, in two papers read in full. Whether the book states it so, and whether it is right about the wrong, is open. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1475](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1475.md) | Gifts oblige giving, receiving and returning | Mauss (1925), [LIT-2191](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2191.md), skimmed in [NOTE-1658](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1658.md) with the introduction, chapter I, the Northwest-coast section and the conclusion read in full. Proposed: the ethnographic half is Mauss's reading of others' fieldwork, and the hau half rests on one informant's text in a translation Mauss calls abridged; the modern half is moral and political argument. It does not say that an unconditional gift exists, that reciprocity needs lost capability, or anything about aid. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1562](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1562.md) v2 | Goods are values only in a bounded life | Cottingham (2014), [LIT-1784](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1784.md), read in [NOTE-1306](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1306.md): a short NDPR review, the record's only report of the book's third lecture and commentaries. Its gloss of the book as "a more altruistic construal of the human condition" runs against the Tanner text, which reads the result as dependence, not altruism. | Active |
| [THEORY-1563](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1563.md) v2 | High existential risk lowers mitigation's value | Thorstad (2023), read in full from the GPI working paper, a penultimate draft ([NOTE-1308](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1308.md)), not compared with the published version. The models are simple and use point estimates; the strongest argument for a time of perils, that advanced AI might end it, is set aside (fn. 7). He concludes that mitigation may be valuable "but perhaps not astronomically so" (§7.4). | Active |
| [THEORY-1565](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1565.md) v2 | Death can harm by deprivation | Luper, SEP "Death" (revised 2026), [LIT-1792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1792.md), read in [NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md) in place of Pitcher (1984, [LIT-1740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1740.md)), which the entry gives in two paragraphs. | [THEORY-1566](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1566.md) v2 | Nullification acts as an exponential discount | Tarsney (2023), read in full from the 2022 working paper ([NOTE-1247](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1247.md)), not compared with the Synthese text. He grants longtermism its normative frame and errs against it on every empirical input. The case survives, and the challenge is "serious" but "not fatal"; on some worldviews it survives only through very small probabilities, and its horizon is thousands or millions of years. Nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1567](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1567.md) v2 | Significance, persistence, contingency multiply | MacAskill, Thomas and Vallinder (2022), [LIT-1778](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1778.md), read in [NOTE-1300](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1300.md) in place of What We Owe the Future ([LIT-1747](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1747.md)). An accounting device that assumes expected-value maximisation and additive features of value; it gives no theory of value and says nothing about who is moved by the value it counts. | Active |
| [THEORY-1568](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1568.md) v2 | Threshold harm answers the non-identity problem | Meyer's SEP entry, Intergenerational Justice, in its 2026 revision ([NOTE-1304](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1304.md)). It surveys and argues: the threshold and disjunctive notions of harm are the author's own position. Scheffler's afterlife conjecture is given at second hand, through McKinnon; longtermism and the empirical work on motivation are absent. | Active |
| [THEORY-1569](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1569.md) v2 | Climate invites intergenerational moral corruption | Gardiner (2006), read in full ([NOTE-1252](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1252.md)). A short programmatic paper: the Pure Intergenerational Problem is drawn from his 2003 paper, which the record does not hold, and seven of the eight corruption strategies are only named. It concerns why policy is hard to make, not what a just policy is, and says nothing about the self. | Active |
| [THEORY-1574](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1574.md) v2 | Existential risk reduction is a global priority | Bostrom (2013), read in full from the published version ([NOTE-1321](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1321.md)). The longtermist text that says most about motivation. Maxipok holds "whenever we act out of an impersonal concern for humankind as a whole", and Bostrom grants that "Unrestricted altruism is not so common" (p. 19). The risk estimates are subjective, and the motivational diagnosis is theory, not tested. | Active |
| [THEORY-1575](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1575.md) v2 | Creating a person neither benefits nor harms | Narveson's late restatement of the person-affecting view (2017), after giving up utilitarianism, read in full ([NOTE-1318](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1318.md)) in place of his 1973 paper. Its second half, on resources and climate, is polemical and rests on popular books. Why future good lives matter is given only through the living: parents', the benevolent's and others' interests. | Active |
| [THEORY-1577](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1577.md) v2 | What matters depends on others surviving us | Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures, [LIT-1779](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1779.md), read in [NOTE-1298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1298.md) in place of Death and the Afterlife ([LIT-1754](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1754.md)). | [THEORY-1604](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1604.md) v2 | Best options now are best for the far future | Greaves and MacAskill, read in full from the 2021 working paper ([NOTE-1302](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1302.md)), not compared with the 2025 chapter the LIT files. The case runs through a benefit ratio against bednets, at least 10^24 expected future beings, and a stakes-sensitivity argument from the axiological to the deontic thesis. The ground is an impersonal good; the agent is "a rational altruistic actor", and nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1610](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1610.md) v2 | Wide person-affecting view solves non-identity | Parfit's last paper (2017), read in full and unfinished by the editor's note ([NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md)). It keeps the No Difference View, retracts his 1984 appeal to an impersonal principle, and offers a person-affecting one in its place. Benefits to future people are owed to whoever will exist, which our choices decide. | Active |
| [THEORY-1626](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1626.md) v2 | Advancing progress rarely rivals risk reduction | Ord's chapter in Essays on Longtermism, read in full from the author's version ([NOTE-1269](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1269.md)), in place of The Precipice. Its aim is "not to argue for longtermism, but to develop a technique for comparing different ways of shaping the longterm future" (p. 7). The results are derived within an idealised model; the empirical aside that people do not discount benefits to others rests on one study the record does not hold. | Active |
| [THEORY-1633](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1633.md) v2 | Risk reduction outweighs settling acceleration | Bostrom's Astronomical Waste (2003), read in full from the author's HTML ([NOTE-1314](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1314.md)), not compared with the journal text. The figures are speculative by Bostrom's own account, and the person-affecting section rests on a guessed chance of radical life extension. Two grounds sit side by side: an impersonal sum on the total view, the good of people now alive on the person-affecting one. Nothing is said about motivation. | Active |
| [THEORY-1649](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1649.md) | Informed consent is a resilient core plus a rim | Eyal, read in [NOTE-1800](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1800.md) (Read). A survey of informed consent in bioethics: why it is required, what it consists in, and its status. §2 canvasses seven candidate justifications — protection (welfare), autonomy, prevention of abusive conduct, trust (forward- and backward-looking), self-ownership, non-domination, and personal integrity — and argues each faces serious objections, with autonomy (dominant since the 1970s) treated at length and found hard to ground as a complete justification. §§3–5 analyze consent itself (behavioral vs psychological; presumed/hypothetical consent), the information requirement, and voluntariness (coercion, undue inducement, "no choice" situations). §8 distinguishes natural-right, legal, epistemic and trust-based accounts of the requirement's status. §9 relates medical consent to sexual, contractual and political consent. §10 argues for a resilient "core" (risky, value-laden, invasive, refused interventions) and a weaker, more overridable "rim". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1650.md) | Mereology fit to a norm can't support it | Mereological implications of the ethics of pregnancy (Dranseika, J Med Ethics 2026), read in [NOTE-1751](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1751.md) (Read), standing in for [LIT-2409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2409.md). Dranseika accepts Devanesan's thesis that a mereology of pregnancy changes the route to an ethical conclusion without entailing it, and adds the converse: normative commitments can legitimately shape which mereology one adopts, but a mereology chosen to fit a commitment is then no independent evidence for it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1652](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1652.md) | OTOF therapy makes infant genetic testing needed | Reisinger and Cederroth, read in [NOTE-1801](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1801.md) (Read). Comments on the FDA's approval (announced 23 April 2026) of Regeneron's Otarmeni, the first gene therapy for a genetic hearing loss (DFNB9, OTOF), and on convergent results from other programmes. Because the therapy is gene-specific and time-sensitive, infants with bilateral hearing loss need genetic diagnosis; clinical sequences should change so that children with profound loss and intact otoacoustic emissions get a genetic diagnosis before a cochlear implant. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1657](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1657.md) | There is no distinctive right to an open future | Millum (2025), read in [NOTE-1734](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1734.md) (Read). Millum argues that there is no distinctive "right to an open future" (Feinberg's rights-in-trust). As a negative right it would rest either on future autonomy or on analogy. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1661](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1661.md) | Circumcision makes a Danish-Jewish family | Dræbel, Sørensen and Meyrowitsch, read in [NOTE-1729](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1729.md) (Read). Twenty semi-structured interviews (2017–2021) with Danish parents of Jewish background (12 fathers, 8 mothers; 18 chose circumcision, 2 did not), analysed with Antonovsky's Sense of Coherence and Davies and Harré's positioning theory, against the background of a Danish public debate (c. 2010–2022) on banning non-therapeutic circumcision of boys (NTCB), including a 2018 citizen proposal to criminalize it. Parents describe NTCB as "inevitable", a taken-for-granted ritual and a rite of passage through which they become Danish-Jewish parents and a family and enrol the son in the family biography, whether or not they are religious. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1666](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1666.md) | Norms may break ties among pregnancy ontologies | Żuradzki (2026), Ethics-first metaphysics: normative considerations as evidence for ontological commitments, read in [NOTE-1744](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1744.md) (Read). A commentary on [LIT-2409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2409.md). Żuradzki accepts Devanesan's thesis that no ontology of pregnancy entails an ethical conclusion but that each constrains which analogies can support one, and argues that the relation is closer: where biological evidence underdetermines competing ontologies, considered normative judgments may themselves count as evidence for choosing between them. This is Dasgupta's "ethics-first" methodology, which Żuradzki extends from personal identity to pregnancy and embryonic identity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1669](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1669.md) | Judge journalism ML data by journalism ethics | Dierickx et al. (2024), A data-centric approach for ethical and trustworthy AI in journalism, read in [NOTE-1736](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1736.md) (Skimmed). Proposes the Accuracy-Fairness-Transparency (AFT) framework for assessing the quality of datasets used to build machine-learning tools in newsrooms, deriving data-quality checks from three core principles of journalism ethics, and placing the work in the shift from model-centric to data-centric AI. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1671](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1671.md) | Child genital surgery only if strictly necessary | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity, read in [NOTE-1799](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1799.md) (Skimmed). Restricting itself to nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery by licensed clinicians on prepubescent children in Global North healthcare systems, and taking no position on criminal law or religious practice outside healthcare, the collaboration argues: there is a near-universal consensus that clinicians may not perform any medically unnecessary genital procedure on endosex girls, however minimal; the sound reasons for that consensus are not benefit–risk calculations but respect for privacy, bodily integrity, developing sexual boundaries and future genital autonomy; those reasons apply equally to intersex children and endosex boys; so clinicians should perform no nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on any child unless it is medically necessary in a strict sense (a serious, time-sensitive threat to physical health, no less invasive or postponable alternative, preserving future choice). They reject the "mental health" defence of early surgery, hold that errors of commission and omission are not symmetric, and invoke Feinberg's "right in trust". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1677](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1677.md) | Recommenders both erode and aid authenticity | Étienne Brown, read in [NOTE-1792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1792.md) (Read). Brown argues that recommender systems affect users' capacity to be their authentic selves, both negatively and positively. He offers a "minimal", multi-dimensional account of authenticity with two dimensions: volitional alignment (Frankfurt, via Rings: acting on first-order desires one reflectively endorses at second order) and self-understanding (an epistemic dimension, relational rather than purely introspective: others' testimony and recommendations are a source of self-knowledge). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1686](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1686.md) | Advance MAID for dementia can't be operationalized | Nix (2024), Operationalizing the Intolerable Suffering Criterion in Advance Requests for MAID for People Living with Dementia in Canada, read in [NOTE-1731](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1731.md) (Read). He argues that, because Carter v. | Proposed |

A human-rights-based instrument covering neurotechnology's whole life cycle, medical and non-medical, and extending to "indirect neural data and non-neural data allowing mental states inferences". Core principles include autonomy (individual and relational) and freedom of thought, protection against manipulation, mental privacy, prior free and informed consent, and specific policy measures for data, employment, consumer products, recommender systems, nudging, sleep marketing, neuromarketing and closed-loop environments. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1713](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1713.md) | LePage wouldn't have ended IVF; law overreacted | Greely (2026), Alabama's LePage decision, the future of ex vivo embryos, and more, read in [NOTE-1733](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1733.md) (Skimmed). | [THEORY-1720](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1720.md) | Users deserve a say in recommender goals | Naudts, Helberger, Veale and Sax (2025), read in [NOTE-1798](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1798.md) (Read). Drawing on Iris Marion Young, they name self-development and self-determination as the values such recommenders should promote, under four democratic conditions: inclusivity, political equality, reasonableness and publicity. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1721](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1721.md) | Adaptive DBS raises autonomy concerns | Muñoz et al. (2020), read in [NOTE-1755](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1755.md) (Skimmed).
